title: How Do You Move From the Text to Sermon Application?
subtitle: How to move from the biblical text to sermon application that is specific, costly, and gospel-driven rather than moralism, with practical steps for preachers.

sections.title: The Gap Between the Text and Tuesday
sections.body:
The explanation is the easy part. The application is where most sermons quietly give up.

We can tell them what the verse meant. We can sketch the context, define the words, trace the argument. And then comes the moment that separates teaching from preaching, the moment we have to say what this demands of the woman in row four whose marriage is failing and the man in the back who has not spoken to his brother in a decade. That is the hardest mile, and most of us coast through it on generalities because the specific is so much more costly to say.

The gap is real. A first century letter to a church in Corinth does not come with instructions for a software engineer in 2026. Crossing that gap honestly is the whole craft. Skip it and you have given a lecture. Fake it and you have given advice. The text was meant to land on a life, and the application is where you let it land or quietly set it down.

sections.title: Application Is Not Moralism
sections.body:
There is a kind of application that sounds biblical and is the opposite of the gospel. We call it being practical.

Moralism is the reflex to end every text with a list of things to do better. Be more patient. Pray more. Serve more. Try harder. It is the message of every religion on earth and the message of none of the prophets. It assumes the problem is effort and the solution is information, and it sends people home with a heavier pack and no new strength to carry it. It is law without grace, and law without grace crushes.

The text does not first tell you what to do. It first tells you what God has done. Real application flows downhill from the gospel, never up toward it. You do not forgive in order to be accepted. You forgive because you have been forgiven a debt you could never repay, and the man who has felt that in his chest can finally release the one who owes him forty dollars. Cut the indicative and the imperative becomes a hammer. I have preached the hammer. I watched good people leave more tired and less free, and I had to repent of it.

sections.title: Get Specific or Get Out of the Way
sections.body:
General application is safe for the preacher and useless to the people. Specificity is the cost you pay for relevance.

Love your neighbor is true and toothless. It convicts no one because it pictures no one. But the neighbor whose music you complain about, the coworker who took credit for your work, the mother in law who criticizes your parenting, now the words have edges, and edges cut, and cutting is the point. The Spirit works through the particular. Vague application lets every person in the room assume it is meant for someone else.

So do the work of imagining the actual people. Not humanity in general. The single mother. The retired man whose calendar emptied out. The teenager performing faith for his parents. Ask what this text demands of each of them on Tuesday, in the kitchen, at the desk, in the silence after the kids are asleep. Then say it plainly. The specific application is riskier because someone will feel exposed. That exposure is not a side effect. It is the text doing exactly what it was given to do.

sections.title: If It Costs Nothing, It Changes Nothing
sections.body:
The application that asks nothing of the comfortable is not application. It is reassurance wearing a clerical collar.

We are tempted, always, to land somewhere that costs the room nothing, because a costless word keeps everyone happy and keeps the offering steady. So we apply the text to people who are not present. We preach against the sins of the culture, the politicians, the other tribe, and the room nods along because it implicates none of them. That is not preaching. That is flattery with a Bible reference.

The true application costs the people in the chairs, and it costs the preacher first. If the text confronts greed, it confronts the building fund and the man who pays for it. If it confronts pride, it confronts the platform you are standing on. The preacher who will not let the text cut him has no business letting it cut anyone else. Self implication is not a rhetorical move. It is the only honest place to stand. We did this. I did this. Now hear what the text says we must do, and let it cost us both.

sections.title: A Working Method for Application
sections.body:
Application is not a flash of inspiration on Saturday night. It is a discipline you can run every week.

Start with the fallen condition the text addresses. Every passage was written into a problem, a brokenness in its first hearers that we still share. Find it. Name the human ache the text is speaking to, and you have found the bridge from then to now, because the human heart has not changed even when everything around it has.

Then ask the text three questions. What does it tell me to believe. What does it tell me to do. What does it tell me to feel. Most sermons stop at the second. The richest application reaches all three, because the gospel reshapes the affections, not only the behavior. A man can do the right thing with a cold heart and the text wants the heart.

Finally, locate it. Put the application in a real room with a real cost and a real person. Then trace it back to the cross so it lands as freedom and not as burden.

And vary who you are speaking to. The same text speaks differently to the skeptic doing the math on whether any of this is true, to the wounded believer who has heard the words and not felt them in years, to the comfortable churchgoer who needs to be unsettled. Name them. Speak to each. The preacher who only ever addresses the settled insider leaves half the room unaddressed and the other half unchallenged. Believe, do, feel. Grounded in grace, aimed at Tuesday, costly enough to be obeyed, spoken to the actual people in the chairs. That is application that leaves the room different than it came in.
